title: customer-firewall-simulated-policy-deviation-notes-2026-03-30
body:
Summary:
We observed a transient control-plane reachability degradation for customer-123 during a scheduled policy rollout. The customer-run firewall applied a policy bundle which our simulator marked as compatible, but production enforcement dropped health-check traffic from the control plane leading to ~7 minutes of degraded telemetry and two Canary failures. This doc captures the timeline, evidence, hypothesis, mitigation steps taken on-call, and proposed runbook/simulator changes.

Why this is interesting/different:
- The simulator validated the JSON policy but did not fully emulate the customer's appliance-specific rule ordering and tag expansion (firewalld zone -> nft translation).
- Result: simulated pass, real-world failure. Lessons here generalize to other on-prem customers with non-standard firewall managers.

Timeline (UTC):
- 2026-03-27 02:05: scheduled policy rollout started via orchestration (deploy job: rw-deploy-4321).
- 02:07: first control-plane health-check failure observed in console (route: cp-heartbeat/customer-123).
- 02:08: on-call page triggered (pager duty).
- 02:09: SRE on-call (Jordan) connected to customer console and requested captures.
- 02:11: tcpdump capture started on customer edge (customer ops): tcpdump -n -i eth0 'host 10.34.5.17 and port 443' -w /tmp/cp-hc.pcap
- 02:12: quick check: orchestration logs show policy applied successfully (status: applied) and returned OK from management API.
- 02:13: packet captures show SYN from control-plane 10.34.5.17 -> customer 10.10.1.2, no SYN-ACK returned; firewall shows RST/DROP counters incrementing on rule id 310.
- 02:16: replicated policy apply in isolated lab VM with same JSON using simulator: simulator reported OK (no deny).
- 02:20: hypothesis formed: rule ordering / implicit zone default drop introduced by customer's firewalld -> nft translation.
- 02:23: customer operations added temporary allow rule for control-plane CIDR/port (append to zone public allow tcp 443 from 10.34.0.0/16)
- 02:30: health-checks recovered; canary green at 02:33.
- 02:40: joint post-mortem call scheduled.

Evidence collected:
- orchestration logs: rw-deploy-4321 (apply returned 200 OK; changeset id a3f5).
- fw appliance rule snapshot (pre/post) saved: /captures/fw-snapshot-pre-2026-03-27.txt, /captures/fw-snapshot-post-2026-03-27.txt
- packet capture: cp-hc-2026-03-27.pcap (SYN no response, then SYN with response after temporary rule).
- nft/iptables outputs from appliance: (excerpt)
  # sudo nft list ruleset
  table inet filter {
    chain input { 
      type filter hook input priority 0; policy accept; 
      iif "lo" accept
      tcp dport 22 ct state established,related accept
      meta skgid 1000 drop # rule id 310 - matches tag applied by orchestration
    }
  }
- firewall management logs show orchestration added a tag-based rule that matched a broad set of traffic because a tag expansion failed and defaulted to group id 1000.

Hypothesis (root cause):
1) The orchestration system generated the intended policy (JSON) which references a named group "cp-heartbeat-sources".
2) On this customer's appliance, the policy management agent translates named groups into kernel-level selectors via firewalld, which expands to nft meta/skgid when the appliance runs a compatibility shim.
3) Due to an earlier broken group-sync job on the customer appliance (customer ops acknowledged a prior failure RW-4239), the named group resolved to an unintended numeric group (skgid 1000), and the orchestrated rule ended up matching broader traffic (including control-plane health-checks).
4) The simulator operates at a logical level (ACL semantics) and does not simulate firewalld tag->skgid translation and the appliance's default rule precedence, so it reported pass.

Immediate mitigations performed during incident:
- Instructed customer to insert temporary allow rule scoped to control-plane CIDR/port above the problematic rule (customer ops executed at 02:23).
- Triggered orchestrator to roll back the specific ruleset (failed in testing due to idempotency quirk) so temporary allow stayed.
- Created an alert (monitor) to detect anomalous increases in 'rule-matches' for rules tagged as 'auto-managed' (short-term).

Permanent corrective actions proposed:
- Simulator improvements (high priority):
  * Extend simulator to model firewalld/nft translation edge-cases (skgid/meta matching).
  * Add "group-resolve" mode where simulator resolves named groups against a mock group-sync DB and flags when groups are missing or map to numeric defaults.
  * Add a rule-ordering check against known appliance precedence tables (customer-configurable).
- Orchestration changes:
  * Add preflight check: before apply, run policy through an appliance-specific converter and do a dry-run on a lab VM that mirrors the customer's agent (must be part of job rw-deploy-guard).
  * Fail fast if named groups cannot be resolved on the target account (mark job status: preflight-failed).
- Customer-facing ops guidance:
  * Recommend customers enable group-sync healthcheck and expose a read-only group mapping endpoint we can query during rollout.
  * Document known appliance shims (firewalld->nft, vendor X -> custom tag mapping) in private knowledge base.

Runbook updates (draft):
- New checklist item when deploying policy to on-prem customer: 
  1) Verify group-sync last-success < 1h via customer-managed endpoint (curl https://customer-api.example.com/groups/last-sync).
  2) Run rw-policy-sim --target appliance-vendor="firewalld" --resolve-groups; ensure no unresolved groups.
  3) If unresolved groups found, abort rollout and notify customer-ops to refresh sync (ticket template attached).
  4) If rollout proceeds, create temporary preemptive allow rule for control-plane CIDR with explicit priority higher than auto-managed rules; schedule removal after 24h post-verification.
- Add a small troubleshooting section: quick checks for on-call
  * Check packet captures for SYN->no-SYN-ACK pattern between control-plane IPs and customer endpoints.
  * sudo nft list ruleset | grep -n "skgid" or sudo iptables -t nat -L -n | grep <tag>
  * Look for management-agent logs: /var/log/fw-agent/syslog for group-sync errors (ERR group-sync failed)

Commands that helped during debugging (keep):
- tcpdump -n -i eth0 'host 10.34.5.17 and port 443' -w /tmp/cp-hc.pcap
- sudo nft list ruleset > /tmp/fw-ruleset-$(date +%s).txt
- sudo cat /var/log/fw-agent/group-sync.log | tail -n 200
- nc -vz 10.10.1.2 443  # quick TCP connect test from bastion

Outstanding questions / open investigation items:
- Why did the group-sync job on this particular appliance fail and resolve to skgid 1000? (customer ops investigating historical upgrades applied March 14).
- Are there other customers using the same vendor shim? Run a fleet query for appliances reporting 'firewalld-compat-mode' and prioritize simulator coverage.
- Can we add telemetry (anonymized) to detect numeric-group fallbacks during rollouts? (privacy review required)

Action items (owners + target dates):
- Add group-resolve simulator feature (Priya) - target 2026-04-08
- Orchestration preflight guard implementation (Liam) - target 2026-04-15
- Update on-call runbook with checklist + commands (Jordan) - target 2026-04-01
- Customer ops follow-up to fix group-sync root cause (customer-123) (Maya) - target 2026-03-31
- Fleet scan for 'firewalld-compat-mode' appliances (Carlos) - target 2026-04-05

Notes to self / informal observations:
- Simulator ambiguity has bitten us before but usually on port/zone mismatches. This case is more insidious because a benign-looking numeric fallback silently widened matches.
- Consider adding a small fuzz-test harness that mutates named group resolution to see what policies would do if group members drift.
- Keep the temporary allow removal automated: schedule job to clean up after 24h if health-checks remain green.

Relevant artifacts stored:
- /captures/cp-hc-2026-03-27.pcap
- /captures/fw-snapshot-pre-2026-03-27.txt
- /captures/fw-snapshot-post-2026-03-27.txt
- Confluence draft: CP policy sim improvements (linked above)

Blameless takeaway: the chain-of-trust between orchestration, customer agent, and kernel-level enforcement has a brittle translation layer; simulators must model translation artifacts or orchestration must detect unresolved mappings and fail safe.

If you edit this doc: add any additional packet-analysis snippets, attach the small Python script we used to parse pcap->SYN counts (tools/pcap-syn-stats.py), and push a short note to the customer explaining the temporary allow and planned follow-ups.

End of notes.
